ns2:section.sectionText: METHODOLOGIES FOR GLOBAL MUSIC HISTORY. Networks and entanglement characterize the world around us, emerging from long histories of interaction and exchange across time and space. Music is a powerful interpretive tool for mapping these processes that were tied to broader political, economic, military, or religious forces from the 15th to the 19th century. In this seminar we will explore developments in the burgeoning field of “global music history,” reading core literature from its proponents as well as relevant work in global historiography more generally. Students are therefore encouraged to think interdisciplinarily, taking music as path by which we can historicize the phenomenon of globalization and globalize our approach to history. In this we will work towards uniting theoretical/analytical and historical perspectives, while looking to a wide range of sources from literary descriptions to musical notation, and visual depictions, among others. How can developments in global history further musicological research? What does a history of Western music look like from a global perspective? What is the difference between global music history as an analytical perspective and as a process? How does music contribute to broader social and cultural histories? These are some of the key questions we will attend to in this seminar by looking beyond a single, uncomplicated narrative about the world’s musical pasts, to embrace a complex dialogue of different voices.
